question: When calling a C library function from Go via cgo, you must pass a string into a C function that expects a char*. What happens to the memory you allocate with C.CString, and why is calling C.free on the returned pointer different from letting Go's garbage collector clean it up?
answer: Passing a Go string to a C function requires C.CString, which allocates null-terminated memory on the C heap; because Go's garbage collector cannot see C heap, that pointer must be freed with C.free or it leaks until process exit. C.GoString copies a C string back into a Go string, and C.GoBytes does the same for byte slices. C.CString copies the input, so mutation never crosses the boundary. The trade-off is a per-call copy that prevents zero-copy handoff but keeps ownership safe.
diagram:
flowchart TD
  GoStr["Go string (immutable, GC-managed)"] --> CString["C.CString(s) allocates C-heap copy"]
  CString --> CPtr["*C.char pointer to malloc memory"]
  CPtr --> Ccall["C function reads/writes the buffer"]
  Ccall --> Cback["C returns char* (static or malloc)"]
  Cback --> GoCopy["C.GoString copies back into a Go string"]
  GoCopy --> Done["Go string is safe after C returns"]

  CPtr --> Free["C.free(p) releases C-heap memory"]
  Free --> LeakFree["No leak: allocation visible only via explicit free"]

  CPtr --> SkipFree["Forget C.free"]
  SkipFree --> Leak["Memory invisible to GC — leaks until process exits"]
